in_context.text: This is the opening greeting of Jude's short letter. Jude names himself as a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, and he describes his readers by what God has done for them: sanctified by the Father, preserved in Jesus Christ, and called. This sets a secure footing before he warns about ungodly men who had crept in among them.

speaker.text: Jude, who calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James. Traditionally he is the Judas listed with James among Jesus' brothers (Matthew 13:55, Mark 6:3).

audience.text: Believers the letter does not locate, described only as sanctified, preserved, and called. False teachers had slipped in among them.

what.text: Jude introduces himself humbly as Christ's servant rather than by any title, and he greets his readers as people whom God has set apart, kept in Christ, and called. The greeting continues with a prayer that mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to them.

events.text: This is a letter greeting, not a narrative, so it describes no event. It addresses a time when ungodly men had already crept into the church.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 65-80, by Jude the brother of James and of Jesus. Scholarly view: dates range from the 50s to the early second century; some think a later follower wrote in Jude's name, while others defend Jude's authorship.

where.text: The letter does not say where it was written or where its readers lived. Its many references to Israel's history and Jewish tradition suggest readers who knew them well.

purpose.text: Jude identifies himself and reminds his readers of their standing with God before urging them to contend for the faith against men who turned God's grace into an excuse for immorality.

big_picture.text: The letter opens with believers 'preserved in Jesus Christ' and closes praising 'him that is able to keep you from falling' (1:24), while also telling them to 'keep yourselves in the love of God' (1:21). Other Scripture also speaks of believers 'kept by the power of God through faith' (1 Peter 1:5) and of Jesus praying that the Father would 'keep them from the evil' (John 17:15).

for_readers.text: Before any warning, Jude grounds his readers in what God has done: he called them, set them apart, and keeps them. Being called is God's work, 'not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace' (2 Timothy 1:9).

why_it_matters.text: The word is doulos, a slave or one in bondage to another. Jude, traditionally one of Jesus' brothers, introduces himself as Christ's servant, as Romans 1:1 and 2 Peter 1:1 also open.

The word means to watch over, guard, keep, or preserve. Jude uses the same verb for the rebel angels 'reserved' for judgment (1:6) and for believers who must 'keep yourselves in the love of God' (1:21).
In the New Testament this word is always used of God's call. Here, as in Romans 8:28 and 1 Corinthians 1:24, it means called to salvation.

The lexicon lists the word in this verse as ēgapēmenois, 'loved', from agapaō. It is used of God's love toward people (Romans 8:37), which fits Jude's later call to 'keep yourselves in the love of God' (1:21).
The lexicon lists this James as 'the Lord's brother', the same James named in Galatians 1:19 and James 1:1. That points to Jude as another of Jesus' brothers.

takeaway.text: Jude starts not with the danger but with God's hold on his people: they are set apart by the Father, kept in Jesus Christ, and called. The God who keeps them is the one 'able to keep you from falling' (1:24).

resolved.reason: It states as fact that Jude is 'listed among Jesus' brothers,' but the cited author source says only that he is traditionally identified with the Judas named among Jesus' brothers. The card presents a traditional identification as settled.
resolved.fix: claim rewritten to match its sources
